We are a team of Mechatronics Engineering students focused on integrating embedded systems, hardware prototyping, software design, and physical modeling to develop functional engineering solutions for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

summary:
Aurora is a health monitor for astronauts on long-duration missions, where no doctor is on board and messages to Earth are delayed. A wearable prototype streams live data over USB to a web app: an ESP32 with ECG, skin conductance, temperature, cabin-pressure, and motion sensors. Its screen centers on an interactive 2D/3D anatomical body, based on MRI-derived BodyParts3D anatomy. Each vital sign appears exactly where it is measured, with a green, amber, or red status, a trend line, and a plain-language normal range.

Every 2 seconds, Aurora computes a full cardiac analysis from real heartbeat timing (heart-rate variability, stress index, QTc and ECG-derived breathing) and checks 28 rules. Each alert comes with a clear action and an animated, timed guide: breathing exercises, cooling, the cabin-leak protocol, or a post-fall “Are you OK?” check. Thresholds come from clinical ranges and NASA’s open Inspiration4 data.

Aurora lets crews spot problems early and act on their own, without medical training. As missions move farther from Earth, that autonomy becomes essential.
details:
What it does and how it works

Aurora is a health monitor for astronauts on long-duration missions, where no doctor is on board and messages to Earth can take minutes. It has two parts:

  • Wearable prototype: an ESP32 with five real sensors:
    • AD8232 ECG, sampled at 200 Hz;
    • GSR skin-conductance sensor;
    • thermistor for body temperature, calibrated with two measured points;
    • BMP180 for cabin pressure;
    • ADXL345 accelerometer.
  • Web app: it reads the ESP32 live over USB. The firmware sends the filtered ECG waveform, the exact time of every heartbeat, and updated metrics every 2 seconds.

The screen is built around an anatomical human body. Each body zone shows a green, amber, or red status. Tapping a zone opens a close-up, in 2D or as a rotatable 3D model built from real MRI-derived anatomy (BodyParts3D). Every measurement is pinned to where it is actually taken (heart, fingertip, wrist, forehead) and shown with:

  • its value and a trend line;
  • its plain-language normal range;
  • whether it comes live from a sensor, from manual entry, or from a reference dataset.

From the heartbeat timing, the app computes a full cardiac analysis every 2 seconds:

  • HRV in the time domain (SDNN, RMSSD, SDSD, pNN50);
  • Poincaré SD1/SD2 and the Baevsky stress index;
  • frequency-domain LF/HF;
  • QT corrected with the Bazett, Fridericia, and Framingham formulas;
  • respiration rate derived from the ECG.

An sEMG mode measures muscle activity and fatigue (MAV, RMS, waveform length, mean frequency). A 32-test suite checks every formula against hand calculations and signals with known answers.

Aurora also tells the astronaut what to do next. 28 recommendation rules are triggered by the data:

  • 4-7-8 breathing when stress rises;
  • a cooling protocol for heat stress;
  • the 15-15 rule for low glucose;
  • a cabin-leak procedure when pressure drops;
  • a 15-second “Are you OK?” check after a fall, which alerts the crew if nobody answers.

Each recommendation comes with an animated, timed step-by-step guide. A built-in reaction-time test (5 taps) detects reduced alertness from sleep loss.

Benefits and intended impact

  • No medical training needed: astronauts can understand their status in seconds.
  • Autonomy: decisions can be made on board without waiting for Earth.
  • Early detection: stress, fever, fatigue, dehydration, or a failing sensor show up before they become emergencies.
  • Honest data: a loose electrode is detected and reported, never shown as a heart problem.
  • Beyond space: the same approach can serve remote or isolated environments on Earth, such as Antarctic stations, submarines, rural clinics, and home monitoring.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Hardware: ESP32, AD8232, GSR V1.2, NTC thermistor circuit, BMP180, ADXL345.
  • Firmware: C with ESP-IDF and FreeRTOS. It runs a 200 Hz sampling task with IIR filters (60 Hz notch, 0.5–35 Hz band-pass) and a Pan-Tompkins-style R-peak detector.
  • Web app: JavaScript, React and Vite; Three.js for the 3D anatomy; Web Serial API for the USB link; SVG for the 2D anatomy, charts and animations.
    • NASA OSDR Inspiration4 blood, cytokine, transcriptomics and cabin-microbiome data (OSD-575, OSD-569, OSD-573);
    • a SANS neuro-ocular rodent study (OSD-817);
    • MMASH, SWELL-KW, sleepstudy and Fitbit.

Creativity

  • The body is the interface: instead of a dashboard of numbers, every reading is placed exactly where it is measured, in 2D and 3D.
  • Built on real hardware: the system is driven by working sensors, not typed-in values. It includes calibration from real measurements and automatic detection of sensor faults.
  • It always proposes an action: every alert comes with a recommendation and an animated guide.
  • Demo scenarios: fever, cabin leak, fall, loose electrode, and others can be triggered on demand, so the full system can be explored without hardware.

Factors the team considered

  • Users: astronauts are not doctors, so text is plain language with the technical term second.
  • Communication delay: the app works fully on board, without depending on Earth.
  • Calm under alarm: critical states are unmistakable without causing panic.
    • status is never shown by color alone (every state also has an icon and a word);
    • text meets WCAG AA contrast;
    • keyboard navigation and a reduced-motion option are supported.
    • Simulated values are labeled as simulated, and reference datasets as reference. Thresholds come from clinical ranges and published data, and a rodent study is not presented as human data.
    • We used AI to accelerate the process, correct programming errors, and help us with guidance on making the user interface.
  • Open licensing: the 3D anatomy is BodyParts3D (CC BY 4.0) and is credited in the app.
